newsitem.title: USA: Talks held to settle Argentina "dirty war" suit.
newsitem.headline: Talks held to settle Argentina "dirty war" suit.

text.p: Settlement talks were held in a landmark lawsuit brought by a former Argentine charging Buenos Aires with human rights violations during the "dirty war" against leftists, lawyers said on Tuesday.

As a result of the negotiations, federal Judge Robert Takasugi ordered the trial -- the first in which a foreign government will be sued in the United States for crimes committed on foreign soil -- postponed until Sept. 12.

"Argentina and the Siderman family are involved in the settlement process that started over the weekend and is still continuing," said Paul Hoffman, an attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California.

Jose Siderman, now a U.S. citizen, claims Argentina's military dictatorship subjected his family to false arrest, imprisonment, torture and unlawful seizure of more than $25 million in assets between 1976 and 1983. He is seeking an unspecified amount of damages.

Siderman first filed the lawsuit in 1982 and won a default judgment of $2.7 million. But Argentina won a reversal from an appeals court that found foreign governments immune from being sued in the U.S. courts.

Siderman, represented by the ACLU, then took the case to the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, which re-instated the case on the grounds that Argentina had waived its immunity by pursuing Siderman in the U.S. courts.

"Argentina tried to thwart our laws and misuse our court system to continue its persecution of the Siderman family in the United States," Hoffman has said. "By doing so, Argentina must be held accountable for all of its acts of repression and persecution of this innocent family."

Siderman's lawsuit claims Argentine soldiers kidnapped him on March 24, 1976, the night the military staged a bloody coup. He alleges he was taken by hooded soldiers to an unknown location and brutally tortured. He was released after a week but told he would be killed if he did not leave the country.

He claims the Argentine government continued to pursue him even after he left, issuing international warrants for his arrest and suing him in Los Angeles Superior Court. The appeals court ruled that lawsuit waived Argentina's immunity.
